prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and biologically active forms of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place GLP-1 first, and that agreement is not what persuades me. The scientific case does. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its actions in humans, to receptor agonists with proven benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The claim is specific rather than a career body of work. It has been confirmed in human physiology, randomized outcome trials and routine care, so recognition would be timely, arguably pressing. Holst (human incretin physiology and GLP-1 secretion and action), Drucker (proglucagon-derived peptide biology, GLP-1 and GLP-2, translation) and Mojsov (the active peptide and its synthesis) give a coherent three-person discovery prize within the supplied credited names.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the weak point. Habener, whose work on the proglucagon gene and GLP-1 is closely tied to the discovery of the active peptide, is not among the credited names, and Mojsov's priority is contested in the public record. I cannot resolve that contest from the supplied evidence. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's industrial peptide engineering (liraglutide, semaglutide) is what actually produced the drugs, so a physiology-focused citation could be criticised as honouring the hormone and not the medicine. If the committee judges the allocation too contested, B050 is the cleaner two-person fallback, at the cost of more indirect medical impact.

responses.point: Perlmann treats GLP-1 as a specific chain from hormone biology to drugs, backs Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the most defensible trio, and sees Knudsen's drug-development role as sitting awkwardly with a three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on keeping the citation tied to the discovery of the physiology and the active peptide. I would qualify one thing. Leaving out Knudsen is a substantive choice and not a neutral one, because the drugs exist through her group's work on half-life extension. The citation wording should therefore say plainly that it honours the discovery of GLP-1 biology and its therapeutic principle, and the committee should note openly that development credit is being left to other recognition.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also ranks GLP-1 first, but favours a mechanistically clean, compact attribution and places cGAS-STING fourth as an original mechanism linking innate immunity to autoimmunity and cancer.
responses.response: I accept the preference for compact, bounded attributions, which is part of why I favour the UPR as my second choice. On cGAS-STING (B021) I would qualify your position. The mechanism is original and Chen/Barber is a compact pairing, but clinical benefit of STING modulation is not yet established, only three of six members ranked it, and your own view that the credited trainees carry lesser weight shows the credit boundary is less settled than for GLP-1. I would not move it ahead of the alternatives I have listed.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks GLP-1 first but raises that Habener is missing from the credited names, and gives the optogenetics case (B034) third as a tool of very high originality and impact, while placing the UPR only seventh.
responses.response: I share the Habener concern and treat it as a limit on what this list allows, not as a reason to demote the candidate. On optogenetics I disagree with ranking it above the UPR. I accept the methodological impact, but six credited names for three slots leaves Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenbock out in any configuration, and the link to disease is still early. The UPR has a clean two-person attribution and a pathway that bears on diabetes, neurodegeneration and secretory physiology. I see it as the stronger second choice, though I would hear your reasons for placing it seventh.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first, sees Knudsen as more naturally recognized separately, and supports CAR-T (Sadelain, June, Rosenberg) as a mature new therapeutic modality, with the caveat that Eshhar and other early CAR originators are not credited.
responses.response: I accept that CAR-T is a major candidate. I placed it fifth for two reasons. The missing early CAR originators weaken a fair allocation, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer work is arguably a separate achievement from CAR engineering, as Perlmann's two-person variant implies. I would not call it a weak case, and it may reasonably become a second prize part if GLP-1 is narrowed to two names. I would want that discussed explicitly, because it changes the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether Habener's omission from the credited names makes the GLP-1 allocation unsafe, and whether Mojsov's priority claim withstands scrutiny.
Whether the citation should honour discovery of the physiology and active peptide or also the drug-development side (Knudsen), and whether a two-part prize is needed to cover both.
Whether B050 or B003 is the stronger second choice if the committee wants a two-part configuration, given the three-person ceiling.
How much weight to give mTOR (B006) when Hall, Schreiber and Sabatini are differently supported and the allocation is unsettled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B022. For disclosure, I co-authored roughly twenty works with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on topics unrelated to the candidates; I also worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow, and he is not a candidate in the shortlist. I do not see either as requiring recusal.
